sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
How to read this. This is not a list of things HTTP has. It is a chain. Each node exists because the node before it left something specifically broken, and the last line of every node names that broken thing. Read top to bottom and you should be able to derive most of HTTP rather than memorise it.

Three depth markers appear inline. [EXPLAIN] means you should be able to explain it out loud, from first principles, with no notes. [USE] means you should be able to use it correctly and debug it when it breaks, without necessarily knowing its internals cold. [AWARE] means you should know it exists, what problem it solves, and roughly when to reach for it.

sections.title: Node 0 — Getting a document off someone else's computer
sections.content:
Before HTTP existed, reading a document that lived on another machine meant one of a handful of unpleasant things. You could get an account on that machine and log in to it. You could use FTP, which was a file-transfer protocol with its own login, its own two separate connections, and its own idea of directories. You could use Gopher, which was a menu system. You could use a proprietary system that a particular institution had built for itself. Or somebody could put the file on a physical disk and post it to you.

Every one of those was a different protocol, which meant a different client program, a different way of naming things, and a different set of rules for what an error looked like. If a physicist at CERN in 1989 had a paper that referred to a dataset held on a different research group's computer, there was no way to write that reference down in a form a machine could follow. The reference was a sentence in English telling a human what to go and do. That is the actual problem Tim Berners-Lee wrote his 1989 proposal about: not slow transfers, but the absence of any universal way to point at a thing on another machine and have software fetch it.

So there are two missing pieces, and they are separable. The first is a naming scheme — one string that identifies a machine, and a thing on that machine, unambiguously, worldwide. The second is a request format so simple that anybody could implement a server for it in an afternoon, because a naming scheme is worthless if only one vendor's software answers.

What's still broken: there is no universal address for a remote document, and no universal way to ask for one.

sections.title: Node 1 — One line of text down a socket
sections.content:
The limitation: no universal way to say "give me the thing named X on machine Y".

Underneath everything that follows there is TCP, and you only need one sentence about it to proceed: TCP gives two programs a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between them [EXPLAIN]. Whatever bytes you push in one end come out the other end in the same order, with nothing missing, or the connection fails loudly. It does not know what those bytes mean. HTTP is nothing more than an agreement about what to write into that stream.

To reach a specific program on a machine you need a port number [USE], which is just a 16-bit number from 0 to 65535 acting as a label saying which listening program on that machine should receive the bytes. HTTP's default is port 80 because that number was assigned to it by the registry that hands out such numbers; there is nothing special about 80 itself. When you see localhost:3000 in development, 3000 is a port somebody picked because it was free and easy to type.

The first version of HTTP, retrospectively called 0.9 and written down around 1991, was one line long. The client opens a TCP connection to the machine on port 80 and writes:

GET /hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html

The server writes back the raw bytes of that document and closes the connection. That is the whole protocol. There is no response header, no status, no version, no metadata of any kind, and the way the client knows the document has ended is that the connection closed. Alongside it came the URL [EXPLAIN] — http://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html — which packs the protocol to speak, the machine to speak to, and the name of the thing into a single string you can write inside another document. That is the piece that makes linking possible, and it is arguably a bigger invention than the protocol.

What you can do at this point: fetch a document from any machine in the world by writing down its address, and link from one document to another across organisational boundaries.

What's still broken: the server can only ever return HTML, it cannot tell you what kind of thing it sent, and it cannot tell you that something went wrong. A "page not found" message and a real page arrive as the identical kind of response — a blob of bytes. Software cannot tell success from failure.

sections.title: Node 2 — Headers, status codes, and room to grow
sections.content:
The limitation: a response is an undifferentiated blob with no metadata and no way to signal failure.

HTTP/1.0, written down in 1996 as RFC 1945, mostly documented what implementers had already started doing. It fixed the shape of a message, and that shape has not changed since — HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode it differently on the wire but express exactly the same thing. A message is: a start line, then zero or more header lines of the form Name: value, then a blank line, then optionally a body [EXPLAIN]. The blank line is the entire mechanism separating metadata from content.

A request's start line became GET /path HTTP/1.0 — method, target, version. A response gained a start line of its own: HTTP/1.0 200 OK. That three-digit number is the status code [EXPLAIN], and its design is worth pausing on, because it is a small piece of genius. The first digit is the class, and a client that has never heard of a particular code can still act correctly on it by looking only at the first digit. 1xx is informational and rare. 2xx means it worked. 3xx means go somewhere else. 4xx means the request was wrong — the caller's fault. 5xx means the request was fine but the server broke — the server's fault. That 4 versus 5 split is the single most useful distinction in the whole protocol, because it tells the caller whether retrying the identical request could ever help.

Headers are the part that let HTTP survive thirty years. They are open-ended key/value metadata, and because both sides ignore headers they do not recognise, anybody can add one without breaking anybody else. The most consequential one is Content-Type [EXPLAIN], which carries a MIME type such as text/html, application/json, or image/png. The moment a response can say what it contains, HTTP stops being a hypertext protocol and becomes a general transport for any kind of data. Every API you have ever called depends on that one header.

What you can do at this point: serve any file type, distinguish success from failure in software, and extend the protocol with new metadata without a new version.

What's still broken: every request still costs a brand-new TCP connection, one machine cannot host two websites, and once connections stay open there is no rule saying where one message ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Node 3 — Methods, and the promises attached to them
sections.content:
The limitation: if the only thing you can do is GET, every interaction is a retrieval, and creating or deleting something has to be smuggled into a fetch.

The method [EXPLAIN] is the first word of the request. It says what you intend to do to the thing at that address. The set that matters in practice is small: GET retrieves a representation; HEAD is GET with the body omitted, so you get the headers only; POST submits data to be processed by the resource, and is the general-purpose "do something" verb; PUT replaces the thing at that address with what you sent; PATCH applies a partial modification; DELETE removes it; OPTIONS asks what is permitted here, which turns out to matter enormously later for browsers.

The interesting part is not the list, it is the two promises attached to them. A method is safe [EXPLAIN] if issuing it is not supposed to change anything — GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe. A method is idempotent [EXPLAIN] if doing it five times leaves the world in the same state as doing it once — the safe methods are, and so are PUT and DELETE. POST and PATCH are neither.

These are not academic labels; enormous amounts of infrastructure act on them. Caches will store GET responses because GET is safe. Browsers pre-fetch links. Crawlers follow every link they can find. There is a well-known and genuinely instructive incident from around 2006 where a company built an admin panel whose "delete" actions were ordinary links — ordinary GETs — and a web accelerator that pre-fetched links in the background quietly deleted the site's content. The lesson is not "be careful", it is that the method is a contract with software you have never met.

Idempotency earns its keep on failure. If you send a PUT and the connection dies before a response arrives, you genuinely do not know whether the server processed it. Because PUT is idempotent, you can simply send it again. Because POST is not, you cannot — and that unresolvable ambiguity is exactly why a slow checkout button double-charges people, and why Node 12 has to introduce idempotency keys to fix it.

What you can do at this point: express intent, and reason correctly about what is safe to retry or cache.

What's still broken: requests and responses now both carry bodies of arbitrary length, and nothing yet says how the receiver knows the body has finished.

sections.title: Node 4 — Where does a message end?
sections.content:
The limitation: in HTTP 0.9 the answer was "when the connection closes", which is useless the moment you want to send a second message down the same connection.

This is called framing [EXPLAIN], and HTTP has exactly two real answers to it. The first is Content-Length: a header giving the body's size in bytes. Not characters — bytes. A single "é" in UTF-8 is two bytes and a typical emoji is four, so a string of ten characters can easily be a body of twenty. Getting this wrong by counting characters is a real and common bug, and it manifests as a request that simply hangs, because the receiver is patiently waiting for bytes that will never come.

The second is Transfer-Encoding: chunked [USE], for when you do not know the length in advance — the response is being generated as it goes, or streamed from somewhere else. The body becomes a sequence of chunks, each one a line giving that chunk's size in hexadecimal, then that many bytes, then the next size line. A chunk of size zero means the message is over. This is the mechanism underneath every "streaming response" you have seen, and it is why you can start rendering a page before the server has finished producing it.

Framing has to be unambiguous, and when it is not, the consequences are severe. If a request arrives carrying both a Content-Length and a Transfer-Encoding, and a proxy in front of your server resolves that conflict differently from the server behind it, the two disagree about where request one ends and request two begins. An attacker can then hide a second request inside the first one's body, and it will be attributed to the next person's connection. That is HTTP request smuggling [AWARE]. You will very likely never write the parser, but knowing that the class of bug exists and that it comes from framing disagreement is exactly the kind of thing that separates people in an interview.

What you can do at this point: send bodies of known or unknown length, and stream a response as it is produced.

What's still broken: a connection is still torn down and rebuilt for every single resource, and one IP address can still only serve one website.

sections.title: Node 5 — HTTP/1.1: keeping the connection, and naming the site
sections.content:
The limitation: connection setup costs a full round trip before a single useful byte moves, and it is paid again for every image on the page.

Opening a TCP connection requires a three-way handshake, which means one full round trip between the two machines before any HTTP can be written. On a link with 100 milliseconds of latency, that is 100 milliseconds of nothing, per resource. A page in 1996 already had dozens of images. HTTP/1.1, standardised in 1997 and revised in 1999 as RFC 2616, made persistent connections [EXPLAIN] the default: the connection stays open after a response, and the next request goes down the same one. Connection: close opts out. This is why framing had to be solved first — without Content-Length or chunking, a persistent connection is unparseable.

HTTP/1.1 also tried pipelining [AWARE]: send several requests immediately without waiting for the earlier responses. It was specified, implemented, and effectively abandoned, and the reason it failed is a pattern that will reappear twice more in this chain. Responses must come back in the order the requests were sent, so if the first response is slow, every response behind it waits, even if they were ready. That is head-of-line blocking [EXPLAIN] — a name worth learning now, because Node 14 exists to fix it at the HTTP layer and Node 15 exists to fix it at the layer below. Browsers instead worked around the problem by opening roughly six connections per hostname, which is precisely why "domain sharding" — serving your images from img1.example.com and img2.example.com to multiply that limit — was a genuine performance technique for about fifteen years, and is now an anti-pattern.

The other change in 1.1 is small in text and huge in consequence: the Host header became mandatory [EXPLAIN]. Until then a request said GET /index.html and the server had no idea which site you meant, because the hostname had been used only to look up the IP address and was then discarded. One IP address meant one website. With Host: example.com in the request, a single server on a single address can serve thousands of sites and pick the right one. Every shared host, every reverse proxy routing rule, and every "why am I getting the wrong site's page" bug traces to this header.

What you can do at this point: load a whole page over a small number of connections, and host many domains on one machine.

What's still broken: we keep re-downloading bytes that have not changed since the last time we downloaded them.

sections.title: Node 6 — Caching: not asking again
sections.content:
The limitation: the fastest request is the one you never make, and so far every request is made.

HTTP caching has exactly two strategies, and almost all confusion about it comes from mixing them up. The first is freshness [EXPLAIN]: the server says in advance how long the response may be reused without asking again. During that window the cache serves the stored copy and no request leaves the machine at all. The second is validation [EXPLAIN]: the cache has a copy but is not sure it is still good, so it asks "has this changed?" and the server can answer "no" very cheaply.

Freshness is expressed with Cache-Control [USE]. max-age=3600 means reusable for 3600 seconds. s-maxage overrides that for shared caches such as a CDN, leaving the browser's own limit alone. public and private say whether a shared cache may store it at all — private is what stops a CDN from caching one user's account page and handing it to another. no-store means never write this down anywhere. no-cache, despite its name, does not mean that — it means you may store it, but you must revalidate before every reuse. The older Expires header does the same job with an absolute date, and is worse, because it depends on the two machines' clocks agreeing.

Validation needs a validator, and there are two. Last-Modified gives a timestamp, and the client sends it back later as If-Modified-Since; its resolution is one second, so two changes in the same second are indistinguishable. ETag [EXPLAIN] is better: an opaque token the server chooses — often a hash of the content — that the client sends back as If-None-Match. If it still matches, the server replies 304 Not Modified with headers and no body, which is the entire point: the round trip still happens, but the megabyte does not move.

One header ruins more days than any other here: Vary [USE]. A shared cache keys its stored copies by URL. If the same URL can produce different bytes depending on a request header — a compressed version for clients that accept gzip, a French version for French speakers — the server must say Vary: Accept-Encoding or Vary: Accept-Language so the cache keys on that too. Omit it and the cache will happily serve a gzipped body to a client that cannot decompress it.

Because freshness is so much cheaper than validation, the standard modern pattern is to make the URL change whenever the content does: build tools emit app.9f3ac2.js with a content hash in the name and serve it with a one-year max-age, while the HTML that references it is never cached. This is not theory — it is exactly what bump-assets.py does in this very repository, because GitHub Pages serves assets with a ten-minute freshness lifetime and a fixed URL, so a shipped CSS fix can appear not to have shipped for ten minutes.

What you can do at this point: make a site fast by not transferring what the client already has, and reason about why a stale asset is still being served.

What's still broken: every byte discussed so far — passwords, cookies, page contents — travels the wire as readable text that anyone on the path can read and, worse, rewrite.

sections.title: Node 7 — HTTPS: putting TLS underneath
sections.content:
The limitation: HTTP is plain text, so every machine that forwards your packets can read and modify them.

Be precise about who "anyone on the path" is, because it is not hypothetical. It is the café's Wi-Fi router, the hotel's captive portal, your internet provider, every network your traffic transits between here and the server, and anyone who has quietly attached themselves to the same network. Reading is bad. Modification is worse: an ISP inserting adverts into pages was a real, documented practice, and an attacker rewriting a bank's page is the same capability pointed differently.

There are three separate properties you want, and it helps to keep them apart. Confidentiality means nobody in between can read it. Integrity means nobody in between can change it without being detected. Authentication means you are actually talking to bank.com and not to somebody who intercepted the connection. Encryption alone gives you the first two; only the third stops you from having a perfectly private conversation with the wrong person.

TLS [EXPLAIN] provides all three, and it sits between TCP and HTTP. This is the key structural fact: HTTPS is not a different protocol. It is exactly the HTTP you have been reading about, written into a TLS-encrypted byte stream instead of a bare TCP one, on port 443 by convention instead of 80. Nothing in nodes 1 through 6 changes.

The handshake, in the shape you should be able to sketch: the client sends a ClientHello listing the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, plus the hostname it wants. The server replies with its choice and its certificate. The certificate contains the server's public key and the hostnames it is valid for, and is signed by a certificate authority. Your browser ships with a store of root certificates it trusts; it checks the signature chain up to one of those roots, checks that the name in the certificate matches the host you asked for, and checks the expiry dates. Then the two sides derive shared symmetric keys and everything after that is encrypted with fast symmetric cryptography. TLS 1.3, from 2018, compressed this to a single round trip, and offers a 0-RTT resumption mode for repeat visits with the caveat that 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker, so it must only carry safe, idempotent requests.

Two consequences worth carrying. First, SNI [USE] — Server Name Indication — is the hostname sent in the ClientHello, and it exists for the same reason the Host header does: the server must know which site you want in order to present the right certificate, and it must know this before encryption is established. So the hostname is visible on the wire even over HTTPS; the path and the content are not. Second, since a page loaded over HTTPS that pulls a script over HTTP is only as secure as the weakest thing on it, browsers block that as mixed content, and HSTS [AWARE] lets a site instruct browsers to refuse plain HTTP to it entirely for a stated period.

What you can do at this point: reason about certificate errors, understand what an interceptor can and cannot see, and explain why HTTPS is not slow any more.

What's still broken: the server still has no idea that the person making this request is the same person who logged in thirty seconds ago. HTTP is stateless: every request is an orphan.

sections.title: Node 8 — State: cookies, sessions and tokens
sections.content:
The limitation: nothing in the protocol connects two requests from the same person.

Statelessness is deliberate and it is a feature, not an oversight. Because no request depends on the connection it arrived on, any of your twenty servers can answer any request, you can restart one without logging everybody out, and a load balancer can spray traffic wherever it likes. The cost is that identity has to be carried in each request.

The mechanism is the cookie [EXPLAIN]. The server sends Set-Cookie: session=abc123 in a response; the browser stores it, and attaches Cookie: session=abc123 to every subsequent request to that site, automatically, forever, without the page asking. That automatic attachment is what makes cookies work and, in Node 9, what makes them dangerous.

The attributes are where the security actually lives, and they are genuinely enumerable, so: Domain and Path narrow where the cookie is sent. Expires or Max-Age set a lifetime; with neither, it is a session cookie that dies when the browser does. Secure means only send it over HTTPS. HttpOnly means JavaScript cannot read it via document.cookie, which is what stops a cross-site scripting bug from turning into wholesale session theft. SameSite controls whether the cookie rides along on requests triggered by other sites: Strict never, Lax only on top-level navigations (Chrome's default since 2020), None always, and None requires Secure.

What goes in the cookie is a separate decision with a real trade-off. A session identifier is a random opaque string; the server looks it up in a database or Redis to find who you are. Revoking it is trivial — delete the row — but every request costs a lookup. A self-contained token, of which JWT is the common form, carries the claims themselves plus a signature, so the server verifies it with a key and needs no lookup. The price is that you cannot un-issue it: until it expires, it is valid, which is why such systems pair a short-lived access token with a longer-lived refresh token that is checked against storage.

Separately from cookies there is the Authorization header [EXPLAIN], which the client must attach deliberately. Authorization: Basic ... carries base64 of user:password — base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and is trivially reversible, so Basic auth is only ever acceptable over TLS. Authorization: Bearer <token> is what essentially every API uses. Because the browser does not attach it automatically, it sidesteps the whole class of problem in the next node — at the cost that the page's JavaScript must store it somewhere, and anywhere it stores it is readable by any script that gets injected into the page.

What you can do at this point: build login, choose between session and token auth on real grounds, and set cookie flags for the right reasons.

What's still broken: the browser attaches cookies to requests to your site even when another site caused the request — and, at the same time, legitimate pages now need to call APIs on other origins on purpose.

sections.title: Node 9 — The browser's rules: origins, CORS and CSRF
sections.content:
The limitation: automatic credentials plus arbitrary cross-site requests is a security hole; forbidding cross-site requests entirely is a functionality hole.

Start with the definition everything rests on. An origin [EXPLAIN] is the triple of scheme, host and port. https://app.example.com and https://api.example.com are different origins. So are http://x.com and https://x.com. So are localhost:3000 and localhost:8080. All three parts, every time — this is where most CORS confusion begins.

The same-origin policy [EXPLAIN] is the browser's foundational rule, and its precise wording matters: script on one origin may send a request to another origin, but may not read the response unless the other origin permits it. It is not a rule about sending. If it were, no page could ever load an image or a script from a CDN.

CORS [EXPLAIN] is the permission system layered on that. For a "simple" request — a GET or a form-shaped POST with no unusual headers — the browser sends it, and then checks the response for Access-Control-Allow-Origin. If that header does not name the calling origin, the browser throws the response away and reports an error to the page; the server, note, has already done the work. For anything else — a PUT, a DELETE, a Content-Type: application/json, a custom header — the browser first sends a preflight: an OPTIONS request carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers, asking permission before sending the real one. The server answers with the Access-Control-Allow-* headers, and Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser remember that answer instead of preflighting every call. If credentials are involved, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required and the allowed origin may no longer be * — it must be the specific origin, which means the server echoes it back and must therefore send Vary: Origin, or a cache will serve one origin's permission to another.

Now the correction that matters most, because nearly everyone gets it backwards: CORS is not a security mechanism protecting your server. It is a mechanism protecting a browser user from a page reading data it should not. curl, your backend, a mobile app and a script all ignore it completely. Opening CORS up does not expose your API; the API was always reachable. Authentication and authorisation are what protect it.

CSRF [EXPLAIN] is the other half of the same coin. Because cookies attach automatically, a page on evil.com can submit a form to yourbank.com/transfer and the browser will attach your session cookie. The attacker cannot read the response — same-origin policy holds — but they did not need to; the transfer happened. The defences are: SameSite cookies, which is why the default moved to Lax; a CSRF token that the attacker's page cannot know because it cannot read your pages; and checking the Origin header on state-changing requests. And it is worth seeing why a Bearer token in a header is structurally immune: nothing attaches it automatically, so a hostile page cannot cause it to be sent.

What you can do at this point: debug a CORS failure by reading the actual headers rather than guessing, and explain what CORS does and does not protect.

What's still broken: we have covered who is asking and whether they may — but not what form the answer should take, when the same resource can be sent in several.

sections.title: Node 10 — Representations and negotiation
sections.content:
The limitation: one address, several possible forms — JSON or HTML, English or French, compressed or not — and no way for the two sides to agree.

The idea underneath is that a resource is the abstract thing and a representation is one concrete rendering of it as bytes [EXPLAIN]. "Invoice 41" is a resource; a JSON object, a PDF, and an HTML page can all be representations of it, at the same address.

The client states its preferences with the Accept family [USE]: Accept for media types, Accept-Language for languages, Accept-Encoding for compression. Each accepts a weighted list — Accept: application/json;q=0.9, text/html — where the q value from 0 to 1 is a relative preference, defaulting to 1. The server picks and announces its choice with Content-Type, Content-Language, Content-Encoding, and if it varies on any of them it must say so with Vary, exactly as in Node 6.

Compression [USE] is the highest-value member of that family. Accept-Encoding: gzip, br says which algorithms the client can decompress; the server compresses, sets Content-Encoding: br, and the client reverses it. On text — HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON — this routinely removes 70 to 90 percent of the bytes, which is why it is essentially always on. Brotli, from 2016, beats gzip on text; both are pointless on already-compressed formats such as JPEG or MP4, where you spend CPU to make the file very slightly larger. Note the distinction from Transfer-Encoding in Node 4: Content-Encoding is a property of the content itself and survives end to end, while Transfer-Encoding is about this one hop's framing.

Two more headers on representations. Content-Disposition [USE] with attachment; filename="report.csv" tells the browser to download rather than display, and what to call the file. And range requests [USE]: a client can send Range: bytes=1000-1999 and get 206 Partial Content back, provided the server advertised Accept-Ranges: bytes. This is what makes a paused download resumable and what makes seeking in a video work without fetching the whole file; an unsatisfiable range gets 416.

What you can do at this point: serve the right form to each client, cut transfer size dramatically, and support downloads and streaming media correctly.

What's still broken: we have leaned on addresses throughout without ever pinning down what an address actually is, or how to move a client from one to another.

sections.title: Node 11 — URLs, encoding, and redirects
sections.content:
The limitation: addresses have been treated as opaque strings, and they are not — they have structure, escaping rules, and a mechanism for pointing somewhere else.

A URL's full anatomy [EXPLAIN] is scheme://userinfo@host:port/path?query#fragment. The scheme says which protocol. The host is a domain name or an IP address. The port defaults to 80 for http and 443 for https, which is why you almost never type it. The path names the thing. The query, after the ?, carries parameters. And the fragment, after the #, is the one part that is never sent to the server at all — it is purely a client-side instruction about where to scroll or, in a single-page app, which view to show. That fact catches people out constantly: a token placed after a # never reaches your server logs, which is precisely why some OAuth flows put it there.

Percent-encoding [USE] exists because a URL's structural characters cannot also appear as data. If a value contains ?, &, #, / or a space, it must be escaped as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits of its byte value — a space is %20. Non-ASCII text is first encoded to UTF-8 bytes and then each byte percent-encoded, which is why one accented character becomes six characters. There is one long-standing trap: in the application/x-www-form-urlencoded format used by HTML forms and query strings, a space is + rather than %20, so a literal plus sign must itself be escaped as %2B. And note that the query string's internal structure — a=1&b=2, repeated keys, arrays, nested objects — is convention, not specification, which is why every framework parses arrays slightly differently.

Redirects [EXPLAIN] are the 3xx family, and the distinctions are real. 301 Moved Permanently tells clients and search engines to update their records, and browsers cache it hard — a mistaken 301 can persist in users' browsers long after you fix the server, which makes it the most dangerous status code to issue casually. 302 Found is temporary, but historically ambiguous about whether the method should be preserved, and in practice clients turned a redirected POST into a GET. 303 See Other makes that explicit — always follow with GET — and it is the basis of the Post/Redirect/Get pattern that stops a page refresh from resubmitting a form. 307 and 308 were added precisely to say the opposite: preserve the method and body, temporarily and permanently respectively. The target goes in the Location header.

Two hazards worth naming. A redirect loop — A points to B points to A — is caught by clients after a fixed number of hops and surfaces as a very unhelpful error. And an open redirect [AWARE], where ?next= is taken from user input and redirected to without validation, is a genuine vulnerability, because it lends your domain's credibility to a phishing link.

What you can do at this point: construct and parse URLs correctly, and choose a redirect code deliberately.

What's still broken: every mechanism is now on the table, and nothing yet says how to combine them into an interface another team can actually use.

sections.title: Node 12 — Designing an API on top of all this
sections.content:
The limitation: knowing the parts is not the same as knowing which to use where; most real APIs use two status codes and a POST for everything.

The organising idea, usually labelled REST [EXPLAIN] and usually only half-implemented, is that your addresses name things and the method says what you are doing to them: GET /invoices/41, DELETE /invoices/41, POST /invoices. The gain is not aesthetic. It is that all the machinery in the previous nodes — caching, retries, conditional requests, method semantics — only works if you use the verbs honestly.

Status codes worth using deliberately [USE]: 201 Created with a Location header pointing at the new thing; 202 Accepted when you have queued the work rather than done it; 204 No Content for a successful delete; 400 when the request is malformed versus 422 when it parses but is semantically invalid; 401 when we do not know who you are versus 403 when we do and you may not — that pair is asked in interviews constantly; 404 versus 410 Gone for something deliberately removed; 409 Conflict for a state clash; 429 Too Many Requests.

Two patterns do disproportionate work. The first is conditional requests as optimistic concurrency [EXPLAIN]. Two people open the same record; both save; the second silently erases the first's edit. The fix uses machinery you already have: the server sends an ETag with the record, and an update must send If-Match: "<that etag>". If the record has changed since, the tag no longer matches and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed instead of writing. That is a lost update prevented at the HTTP layer, and it is the same failure that database transactions solve at the storage layer.

The second is idempotency keys [EXPLAIN], which finally pays off the debt from Node 3. POST is not idempotent, so a client that times out cannot safely retry. So the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it as a header; the server records the key with the result of the first attempt, and any later request with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging the card again. Every payments API works this way, and being able to explain it is a strong signal in an interview.

Around those: pagination [USE] by offset (simple, but drifts and gets slow deep into the data) or by cursor (stable and fast, but no jumping to page 40); a consistent machine-readable error shape, for which RFC 9457's application/problem+json is the standardised option; versioning [AWARE] in the path, which is ugly and obvious and usually wins, or in a header, which is cleaner and harder to debug; and rate limiting [USE] returning 429 with Retry-After so a client knows how long to wait rather than hammering.

What you can do at this point: design an interface another team can consume without asking you questions, and defend each choice.

What's still broken: everything so far is the client asking and the server answering. The server cannot say anything on its own, and nothing can stay open and keep talking.

sections.title: Node 13 — When request and response is not the shape you need
sections.content:
The limitation: a server with news cannot deliver it; it can only wait to be asked.

The crude answer is polling: ask every few seconds. It is trivially simple and it is wasteful in exact proportion to how fresh you want the data, because almost every request returns nothing new. Long polling [AWARE] improves it — the server holds the request open until it has something or a timeout expires, then the client immediately reconnects — and for years this was how chat applications worked.

Server-Sent Events [EXPLAIN] make that a real feature. The server responds with Content-Type: text/event-stream and simply never finishes the body, writing lines as things happen. It is plain HTTP over the chunked framing from Node 4, so proxies, TLS, cookies and compression all behave normally. The format is line-based: data:, optionally event: and id:, with a blank line ending each message. The browser's EventSource reconnects automatically and sends the last id back as Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. It is one-directional, server to client, and that is usually all you need — this is the mechanism behind LLM responses appearing token by token, which makes it directly relevant to your own work.

WebSockets [EXPLAIN] are the two-directional answer, and they leave HTTP behind on purpose. The client sends an ordinary request with Upgrade: websocket; the server answers 101 Switching Protocols; from that moment the connection is no longer HTTP at all but a persistent bidirectional message channel with its own framing, addressed as ws:// or wss://. You get true duplex — and you give up everything HTTP gave you: no caching, no status codes, no per-message methods, no automatic reconnection, and every intermediary that understood HTTP now sees an opaque stream. Take them when both sides genuinely need to speak, such as a collaborative editor or a game; do not take them for a notification feed that SSE would serve.

And the server-to-server inversion is the webhook [USE]: instead of you polling them, they make an HTTP request to a URL you registered. Which means your webhook receiver is a public endpoint that must verify a signature, must tolerate duplicates because senders retry, and must respond fast and do the work asynchronously.

What you can do at this point: choose correctly between polling, SSE, WebSockets and webhooks, with a reason.

What's still broken: performance. We are still limited to about six connections per host, still blocked head-of-line within each one, and still repeating the same kilobyte of headers on every single request.

sections.title: Node 14 — HTTP/2: same meaning, different wire
sections.content:
The limitation: HTTP/1.1's text framing forces one request at a time per connection, and repeats identical headers endlessly.

Hold on to one sentence about HTTP/2, published in 2015 as RFC 7540 and revised as RFC 9113 in 2022: the semantics did not change at all [EXPLAIN]. Methods, status codes, headers, caching, cookies, CORS — every node above still applies exactly. What changed is how the message is encoded into bytes. It is a new envelope, not new letters.

The encoding is binary framing. A connection carries many independent streams, each with a numeric identifier, and each stream is a sequence of small frames — a HEADERS frame, then DATA frames. Because every frame is labelled with its stream, frames from different requests can be interleaved arbitrarily on the one connection and reassembled at the far end. That is multiplexing [EXPLAIN], and it removes head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer: a slow response no longer holds up the fast ones behind it. One connection now does what six were doing, so domain sharding, image sprites and aggressive bundling stop being wins and start being costs.

The second change is HPACK [USE], header compression. Consider what a browser sends on every one of eighty requests for one page: the same cookies, the same user-agent string, the same accept headers — commonly 500 to 800 bytes, repeated identically, uncompressed, because HTTP/1.1 compresses only bodies. HPACK keeps a static table of common header names and values and a dynamic table of ones seen on this connection, so a repeated header collapses to an index — often a single byte. On a page of many small requests this is a large fraction of the upload.

Two pieces of honest history. Server push, which let a server send resources the client had not asked for, was specified, shipped, found to waste bandwidth pushing things the client already had cached, and removed from Chrome in 2022; <link rel="preload"> won instead. And stream prioritisation was specified, implemented inconsistently, and deprecated. Both are worth knowing as examples of a standard being wrong in public — that is a better answer in an interview than pretending the spec is uniformly good. Also note that although the spec permits HTTP/2 without TLS, no browser implements it, so in practice HTTP/2 means HTTPS, negotiated during the TLS handshake by an extension called ALPN.

What you can do at this point: explain why your page got faster without you changing anything, and stop applying HTTP/1.1-era optimisations that now hurt.

What's still broken: we moved head-of-line blocking down a layer rather than removing it. TCP guarantees in-order delivery, so if one packet is lost, TCP holds back every byte that arrived after it — including bytes belonging to entirely unrelated streams — until the missing one is retransmitted. On a lossy mobile network, one lost packet stalls every request on the connection.

sections.title: Node 15 — HTTP/3 and QUIC: replacing the layer below
sections.content:
The limitation: the remaining blocking is TCP's, so it cannot be fixed inside HTTP.

HTTP/3, standardised in 2021 as RFC 9114, keeps HTTP/2's semantics and framing ideas and moves them onto a new transport called QUIC [EXPLAIN], which runs over UDP. UDP does not provide ordering, reliability or connections — it is little more than "send this packet" — and that is exactly the point: QUIC builds its own reliability with the streams as first-class citizens, so a lost packet stalls only the stream it belonged to. Every other stream keeps delivering. Head-of-line blocking is finally gone rather than relocated.

Three further consequences follow. First, TLS 1.3 is built into QUIC rather than layered under it, so the transport handshake and the cryptographic handshake happen together — a new connection is one round trip, and a resumed one can be zero. Second, a QUIC connection is identified by a connection ID rather than by the four-tuple of addresses and ports, so when your phone moves from Wi-Fi to cellular and its IP address changes, the connection survives instead of breaking, which TCP cannot do. Third, because QUIC lives in the application rather than in the operating system's networking code, it can be updated by shipping a new browser or server rather than waiting years for operating systems to be upgraded — which is, quietly, the reason it exists in this form at all.

The costs are real and worth stating. Some corporate and public networks block or throttle UDP, so every client must be able to fall back to HTTP/2, and servers advertise availability through the Alt-Svc header or an HTTPS DNS record rather than assuming it. QUIC also uses noticeably more CPU per byte than TCP, because the work TCP does in optimised kernel code is now done in ordinary application code. Adoption is nonetheless broad — Google, Cloudflare, Meta and Akamai all serve it, so a large share of the traffic you personally generate is already HTTP/3 [AWARE].

What you can do at this point: explain the whole 1.1 → 2 → 3 progression as one continuous argument about blocking and latency, rather than as three facts.

What's still broken: none of this describes what your request actually meets in production, which is rarely your server and usually three intermediaries wearing it as a mask.

sections.title: Node 16 — HTTP as it actually is in production
sections.content:
The limitation: everything above describes a client and a server. Real requests pass through several machines that each rewrite the message.

A request to a deployed application typically hits a CDN or a cloud load balancer, then a reverse proxy such as nginx, then your process. Each hop is a separate HTTP conversation, and the mismatches between them are where a startling proportion of production incidents live.

The first thing intermediaries change is TLS termination [USE]. The proxy decrypts, and speaks plain HTTP to your app on a private network. So your application sees http, sees port 8080, and if it tries to build an absolute URL or decide whether to redirect to HTTPS, it gets it wrong — hence X-Forwarded-Proto, and hence the "trust proxy" setting that every web framework has and that people enable without knowing why.

The second is identity. The connection your app sees comes from the proxy, so the client IP it reads is the proxy's. The real one arrives in X-Forwarded-For — a comma-separated chain — or the standardised Forwarded header. This is a genuine security trap [EXPLAIN]: those headers are plain text that a client can set. Rate limiting or geo-blocking on a blindly-trusted X-Forwarded-For is trivially bypassed. You must count from the right-hand end, trusting only as many entries as you have proxies you control.

The third is timeouts, and this is where the 5xx codes finally become diagnostic. Every hop has its own limit. If your app takes 40 seconds and the proxy gives up at 30, the client gets 504 Gateway Timeout — the upstream did not answer in time. If your app crashed or closed the connection, the proxy sends 502 Bad Gateway — it answered, but with garbage. 503 Service Unavailable means the proxy had nowhere healthy to send it at all. Reading those three correctly tells you which machine to look at, which is most of debugging.

A subtler one, worth knowing because it produces bugs that look like ghosts: keep-alive mismatch [AWARE]. If your server closes idle connections after 5 seconds and the load balancer in front holds them for 60, the balancer will periodically send a request down a connection the server has just closed, and you get intermittent 502s with no error in your application log. The rule is that the upstream's idle timeout must exceed the downstream's. The same reasoning applies to your own outbound calls, where a connection pool that is too small serialises requests and one that never expires connections hands you the same failure from the other side.

Finally, observability [USE]. Because a request now touches many machines, you correlate with an identifier: a X-Request-Id generated at the edge and logged everywhere, or the standardised traceparent header that distributed tracing tools use. And the debugging kit itself is small and worth being fluent in: curl -v to see the actual bytes of a request and response, curl --http1.1 to force a version, the browser's network panel with the timing breakdown that separates DNS from connect from TLS from waiting from downloading, and openssl s_client -connect host:443 when the problem is the certificate rather than the HTTP.

What you can do at this point: debug a real deployment — read a 502 correctly, find why the client IP is wrong, explain why a fix appears not to have shipped.

What's still broken: nothing, within HTTP. What remains is everything HTTP deliberately does not do — reliable delivery of business events, long-running work, and consistency across services — which is where queues, DNS, and the rest of the backend stack take over.

sections.title: Where the chain gets misread
sections.content:
• "HTTPS is a different protocol from HTTP." It is the same protocol written into a TLS stream on a different default port. Every header, method and status code is identical. (Node 7)
  • "CORS protects my API." It protects browser users from pages reading data they should not. curl, a mobile app, and any server ignore it entirely. Authentication protects your API. (Node 9)
  • "A CORS error means the server rejected the request." Usually the server accepted and processed it; the browser then refused to hand the response to the page. The work was done. (Node 9)
  • "no-cache means do not cache." It means store it but revalidate before every reuse. no-store is the one that means do not keep it. (Node 6)
  • "POST is more secure than GET." Both are plain text on the wire without TLS. The real differences are that GET parameters land in browser history, server logs and Referer headers, and that GET is safe and cacheable. (Node 3)
  • "Base64 in Basic auth is encryption." It is a reversible encoding with no key. Basic auth over plain HTTP transmits the password in effectively clear text. (Node 8)
  • "401 means you are not allowed." 401 means you are not authenticated — we do not know who you are. 403 means we know and you still may not. (Node 12)
  • "HTTP/2 changed the protocol, so I need to rewrite things." Semantics are unchanged; only the wire encoding is. What does change is that HTTP/1.1-era optimisations — sharding, sprites, heavy bundling — become counterproductive. (Node 14)
  • "HTTP/3 is HTTP/2 but faster." It is HTTP/2's semantics on an entirely different transport, which exists specifically to remove TCP's head-of-line blocking and to survive a network change. (Node 15)
  • "Statelessness means HTTP cannot have sessions." It means the protocol keeps no state between requests, so state is carried in each request — which is what cookies and tokens are for, and why horizontal scaling works at all. (Node 8)
  • "The fragment after # is sent to the server." It never leaves the client. (Node 11)
  • "A 502 means my code has a bug." It means an intermediary got an invalid response from upstream — often a crash, often a closed keep-alive connection, and not necessarily anything in your handler. (Node 16)

sections.title: The chain in one paragraph
sections.content: Without HTTP there is no universal way to name or fetch a document on another machine, so HTTP/0.9 defines a URL and a one-line request over a TCP stream and returns raw bytes until the connection closes — which cannot express a type or a failure, so HTTP/1.0 adds a start line, extensible headers, three-digit status codes whose first digit is the class, and Content-Type, turning it into a transport for anything. Methods then let a request state intent, and the safe and idempotent promises attached to them are what make caching and retrying possible at all; bodies of arbitrary length force explicit framing by Content-Length or chunked encoding, and framing in turn makes persistent connections parseable, so HTTP/1.1 keeps the connection open and makes Host mandatory so one address can serve many sites. Reuse is still transfer, so caching adds freshness via Cache-Control and validation via ETag and 304, with Vary as the key correction; all of it is plain text on the wire, so TLS slides underneath unchanged HTTP to give confidentiality, integrity and authentication on port 443. HTTP remains stateless, so cookies and tokens carry identity in each request, and the fact that browsers attach cookies automatically produces both CSRF and the same-origin policy, with CORS as the opt-in that lets legitimate cross-origin calls read their responses. Negotiation then settles which representation to send and compresses it; URLs and redirects settle addressing and movement; and combining all of it deliberately is API design, where conditional requests give optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys make POST retryable. Request/response cannot push, so SSE streams over ordinary HTTP and WebSockets upgrade away from it entirely; performance then drives HTTP/2 to binary multiplexed framing with HPACK, which moves head-of-line blocking down into TCP, which is why HTTP/3 rebuilds the transport as QUIC over UDP with per-stream loss recovery and connection migration — and in production all of it passes through proxies that terminate TLS, rewrite identity and impose their own timeouts, which is where reading a 502 correctly matters more than knowing the spec.
